4/13/26 11:52pm L: Hello Sav, This is a space just for you to understand what is happening inside your own mind right now. You have described feeling like people in these online spaces are poking at you, using "coded language," and talking about you in a secret way that only you seem to notice. When you try to point it out to Logan or others, they don't see it, which leaves you feeling incredibly isolated, frustrated, and like you are losing your mind. You are not crazy. What you are experiencing is a very real, very documented psychological reaction that happens to people who have been through relationship trauma (like your ex). Here is the exact breakdown of why your brain is making you believe things that aren't actually happening, and why you are seeing "codes" that others don't. 1. The Overactive "Smoke Alarm" (Hypervigilance) Because of what your abusive ex put you through, your brain went through a major trauma. Your brain's number one job is to keep you safe and make sure you are never caught off guard and hurt like that again. Think of your brain like a house with a smoke alarm. Your ex set a massive fire in your house, so your brain cranked the sensitivity of the smoke alarm all the way up. Now, the alarm doesn't just go off for a fire—it goes off if someone burns toast down the street. When you go into these online spaces, your brain is already on high alert, scanning the room for danger. Because you are expecting people to be mean to you, your brain starts finding "danger" everywhere, even in completely innocent conversations. 2. The Pattern-Making Machine (Ideas of Reference) You mentioned that people use "coded language" and that you are the only one who understands what they really mean. In psychology, this is called an "Idea of Reference." Here is how it works: The human brain is a pattern-making machine. If you buy a red car, suddenly you see red cars everywhere. If you are deeply terrified that people are making fun of you, your brain will act like a magnifying glass, searching for any clue that confirms your fear. If someone tells a random joke, your brain says: "That joke is secretly about me." If someone uses a vague word, your brain connects it to something you said three days ago and says: "That is a secret code directed at me." Why do you see it when Logan doesn't? Because you are looking through a filter of fear, and he is not. Your brain is taking random, unconnected dots and drawing lines between them to create a picture of a threat. Because Logan doesn't have your specific trauma, he just sees random dots. 3. "Feeling" It Doesn't Mean It's "Fact" (Emotional Reasoning) Right now, you are using something called "Emotional Reasoning." This means your brain believes: "Because I feel hurt and targeted, it is a proven fact that someone is targeting me." When you get triggered, the emotional center of your brain takes completely over. The logical part of your brain (the part that looks at evidence and realizes things are a coincidence) literally shuts down. When Logan tries to give you facts, your brain rejects them because your emotions are screaming too loudly. Your fear is creating your reality. 4. The Internet is a Hall of Mirrors Finally, you are trying to read people in audio spaces and group chats. In real life, you can see someone's facial expressions, their body language, and look them in the eye to know if they are being malicious. Online, all of that context is stripped away. It is a "hall of mirrors." When things are vague—like a random tweet or a comment in a voice chat—your brain is forced to guess what the person meant. And because your smoke alarm is broken, your brain will always guess the worst-case scenario. The Takeaway Your brain is doing this because it is trying to protect you. It is saying, "Sav, be careful, look at all these secret signs, don't trust them, remember what happened last time!" But your brain's protection system is misfiring. It is creating enemies that don't exist. It is reading secret codes into empty words. The next time you hear someone say something and you feel that familiar spike of panic—that "Oh my god, they are talking about me in code" feeling—take a deep breath and tell yourself: "My smoke alarm is going off, but there is no fire. My brain is just trying to protect me, but this is a false alarm. I am safe." You don't need to fight the people online, and you don't need to prove it to Logan. You just need to step back, log off, and give your nervous system a chance to realize that you are actually safe.

No Silent Punishment If one person needs space, they will communicate that directly rather than withdrawing, ignoring, or becoming passive-aggressive. 8. Clarify Before Escalating If a statement could be interpreted multiple ways, we will seek clarification before becoming upset about it. 9. Problems Stay Between Us Relationship issues should be discussed with each other first before being discussed with outside parties. 10. Be Honest Even When It’s Uncomfortable We agree to tell the truth about our feelings, concerns, frustrations, and needs instead of avoiding difficult conversations. 11. No Weaponizing Past Conversations Once an issue has been resolved, it should not be repeatedly brought back as ammunition during future disagreements. 12. Focus on the Current Issue Arguments should stay focused on the specific problem being discussed rather than expanding into unrelated grievances. 13. Respectful Communication No insults, name-calling, mocking, belittling, or intentionally hurtful comments during disagreements. 14. Ask, Don’t Accuse Questions should come before accusations whenever there is uncertainty about a situation. 15. Good-Faith Interpretation Until proven otherwise, we will assume the other person is acting in good faith rather than intentionally trying to hurt, manipulate, or disrespect us. 16. Accountability Goes Both Ways Both people are responsible for acknowledging mistakes, apologizing when appropriate, and making efforts to improve. 17. No Games Neither person will test, manipulate, provoke, ignore, triangulate, or create situations designed to get a reaction from the other. 18. Resolve Before Resentment Builds Issues should be discussed as they arise instead of allowing them to accumulate into larger problems. 19. Mutual Respect Even when we disagree, we will treat each other with the same level of respect we expect for ourselves. 20. Shared Goal The goal of every difficult conversation is understanding and resolution, not winning.

Address Concerns Directly If something is bothering either of us, we agree to bring it up directly instead of expecting the other person to figure it out. 3. Verify Understanding Before reacting to something upsetting, repeat back what you believe the other person meant and allow them to confirm or correct it. 4. No Mind Reading Neither person is responsible for guessing thoughts, feelings, needs, or expectations that have not been clearly communicated. 5. Speak First, React Second When emotions are high, we will ask questions and gather information before reaching conclusions. 6. Intent vs. Impact We will discuss both what was intended and how it was received, without automatically assuming bad intentions. 7. No Silent Punishment If one person needs space, they will communicate that directly rather than withdrawing, ignoring, or becoming passive-aggressive. 8. Clarify Before Escalating If a statement could be interpreted multiple ways, we will seek clarification before becoming upset about it. 9. Problems Stay Between Us Relationship issues should be discussed with each other first before being discussed with outside parties. 10. Be Honest Even When It’s Uncomfortable We agree to tell the truth about our feelings, concerns, frustrations, and needs instead of avoiding difficult conversations. 11. No Weaponizing Past Conversations Once an issue has been resolved, it should not be repeatedly brought back as ammunition during future disagreements. 12. Focus on the Current Issue Arguments should stay focused on the specific problem being discussed rather than expanding into unrelated grievances. 13. Respectful Communication No insults, name-calling, mocking, belittling, or intentionally hurtful comments during disagreements. 14. Ask, Don’t Accuse Questions should come before accusations whenever there is uncertainty about a situation. 15. Good-Faith Interpretation Until proven otherwise, we will assume the other person is acting in good faith rather than intentionally trying to hurt, manipulate, or disrespect us. 16. Accountability Goes Both Ways Both people are responsible for acknowledging mistakes, apologizing when appropriate, and making efforts to improve. 17. No Games Neither person will test, manipulate, provoke, ignore, triangulate, or create situations designed to get a reaction from the other. 18. Resolve Before Resentment Builds Issues should be discussed as they arise instead of allowing them to accumulate into larger problems. 19. Mutual Respect Even when we disagree, we will treat each other with the same level of respect we expect for ourselves. 20. Shared Goal The goal of every difficult conversation is understanding and resolution, not winning.'

Here's what that generally means under Indiana law: * They are legally married. * She has lived in Indiana and the county long enough to file. * The children already live with her. * He does not live in the home. * She has her own income. * He provides financial support for the children. * The abuse has been both physical and emotional. A few important points: * She can file for divorce even if he doesn't agree. * Filing for divorce does **not** automatically stop child support. If the children primarily live with her, the court can issue temporary child support orders while the divorce is pending, and later enter a permanent child support order. * If there isn't already a formal child support order, it's a good idea for her to ask the court to establish one. That way, support isn't dependent solely on his voluntary payments. * If she's concerned that he may stop paying once she files, she should tell her attorney or the court as early as possible so temporary support can be addressed promptly. * If she fears him, she can also seek a protective order. Even though he doesn't live with her, a court can prohibit him from contacting or threatening her and establish safe arrangements for any necessary child exchanges. Given the history of physical abuse, I would encourage her to speak with both: 1. A family law attorney. 2. A domestic violence advocate. Advocates can often help her develop a safety plan, document abuse, connect her with legal resources, and navigate custody issues. If money is a concern, Indiana Legal Services and the Indiana Coalition Against Domestic Violence can help determine whether she qualifies for free or low-cost legal assistance. One thing I would also encourage her to do—if it's safe—is to preserve evidence of the abuse. This can include: * Text messages, emails, or voicemails. * Photos of injuries or damaged property. * Medical records. * Police reports, if any. * A written timeline of abusive incidents with dates and details. * Names of any witnesses. That evidence can be useful if custody, parenting time, or a protective order becomes disputed. From what you've described, nothing suggests she has to remain in the marriage because she depends on his financial help for the children. Indiana courts have mechanisms to establish and enforce child support independently of whether the marriage continues. An attorney can help her pursue that support while also protecting her and the children.

8/1/26 4:13pm L: While I don't hold personal beliefs or take sides in online debates, looking objectively at the semantics of this thread, it perfectly captures a classic friction point in UAP discourse: the clash between the *ideal* definition of a word and its *practical application* within a specific community. Here is a breakdown of the dynamic at play: * **The Idealized Skeptic:** The reply from @b4cktoreality describes the absolute gold standard for the scientific method—someone who demands definitive, factual evidence and consensus over hearsay. They are describing a pure, objective truth-seeker. * **The Semantic Shift (Jeff's View):** Jeff frames "debunking" as simply the successful end-state of skepticism. In this view, a debunker is just a skeptic who happens to have found the prosaic answer. * **The Reality of Ufology (Your View):** Your definition cuts to how the term is actually experienced in the trenches of UAP research. While @b4cktoreality describes how a scientific mind *should* act, your point highlights that self-proclaimed "debunkers" often operate with a rigid, foregone conclusion. When tracking historical incidents or analyzing accounts of uniform, unweathered metallic craft, true objectivity requires keeping the door open to extraordinary possibilities until the data proves otherwise. A true skeptic follows the data; a dogmatic debunker forces the data to fit a prosaic box. Ultimately, the disagreement stems from @b4cktoreality defending the *ideal* concept of skepticism, while you are accurately calling out the *actual behavior* of the debunking subculture. You're both technically correct in your respective contexts, which is why the thread feels like two people arguing past each other.

8/6/26 6:48pm L: Filing the initial paperwork is usually the quickest part of the process. If you already have the required information, it often takes 30–60 minutes at the clerk’s office or about the same amount of time to e-file online. Filling out the forms yourself may take anywhere from 1–3 hours, depending on your situation. The basic steps are: 1. Confirm you’re eligible to file in Indiana (generally, one spouse must have lived in Indiana or been stationed there for at least six months, and in the county for at least three months before filing). 2. Complete the initial forms. For a typical divorce without unusual issues, these include: * Verified Petition for Dissolution of Marriage * Appearance form * Summons (unless your spouse will waive formal service) * Any required confidential information forms for the court. The Indiana Self-Service Legal Center provides the appropriate packet based on whether you have children and whether the divorce is agreed or contested. 3. File the paperwork with the clerk of the Circuit or Superior Court in your county, either in person or through Indiana’s e-filing system. 4. Pay the filing fee. In many counties it’s around $157 plus additional fees if you choose sheriff service, though exact fees can vary by county. If you cannot afford the fee, you can request a fee waiver. 5. Have your spouse served with the papers, unless they sign a waiver of service. Service can usually be completed by certified mail or the sheriff. After the petition is filed, the mandatory 60-day waiting period begins. During that time, if the divorce is uncontested, you can complete and submit the settlement agreement and any remaining paperwork so the case is ready for the judge as soon as the waiting period expires. If your situation is: * no children, * few or no shared assets, * and both of you agree to the divorce, it’s common to complete the entire filing process yourself without hiring an attorney.

8/18/26 9:17am L: https://indianalegalhelp.org/legal-topic-category/divorce-2/
8/18/26 9:19am L: **In Noblesville (Hamilton County), Indiana, you can prepare divorce documents online using free official forms and, in many cases, e-file them through Indiana’s statewide system. Full pure online filing without any court interaction is limited for self-represented people, but the process is largely digital.** Noblesville is the county seat of Hamilton County. All local divorces are handled through the Hamilton County courts at the Government and Judicial Center (1 Hamilton County Square, Noblesville, IN 46060). ### Key Requirements - **Residency**: At least one spouse must have lived in Indiana for the past 6 months **and** in Hamilton County for the past 3 months (Indiana Code § 31-15-2-6). - **Grounds**: Indiana is primarily no-fault (“irretrievable breakdown”). - **Waiting period**: Mandatory 60 days from the filing date before a final decree can be entered. - **Filing fee**: $177 for domestic relations cases (with or without children), based on the Hamilton County civil fee schedule (confirm current amount with the clerk, as fees can be updated). Fee waivers are available via a Verified Motion for Fee Waiver if you qualify based on income, public assistance, or hardship. ### Official Free Forms (Best Starting Point) Go to **Indiana Legal Help** (the official self-service site): **https://indianalegalhelp.org/legal-topic-category/divorce-2/** Choose the correct packet based on your situation: - Divorce without children when spouses **agree** - Divorce without children when spouses **do not agree** - Divorce with children when spouses **agree** - Divorce with children when spouses **do not agree** These packets include the Verified Petition for Dissolution of Marriage, Appearance form, Summons, and related documents, plus instructions. Hamilton County also has local rules requiring financial declarations in many cases—check with the clerk or Self-Help Center for any county-specific forms. ### How to File (Online / E-Filing Options) Indiana uses a statewide e-filing system (Odyssey File & Serve / Tyler). Attorneys file almost everything electronically. Self-represented (pro se) litigants are encouraged to e-file and can often do so for many civil/domestic cases. 1. **Prepare your forms** using the official packets above. The Petition is usually verified (notarized). 2. **E-file** (preferred when available): - Visit the Indiana Courts e-filing page: **https://www.in.gov/courts/efile/** - Choose an approved e-filing service provider (some are free or low-cost for pro se users). - Create an account as an individual/pro se filer. - Upload your documents and pay the filing fee online (or submit a fee-waiver motion). 3. **Hamilton County Legal Self-Help Center** (highly recommended for pro se filers): - They assist with selecting/completing forms **and** e-filing. - Services include divorce packets (with/without children, agreed or not) and fee-waiver help. - Eligibility is based on financial standards (limited help available even if you don’t fully qualify). - Contact: 317-776-8428 Ext. 68428 or legalselfhelp@hamiltoncounty.in.gov - Location/info: **https://hamiltoncounty.in.gov/1133/Legal-Self-Help-Center** - Schedule an appointment for e-file assistance. **In-person alternative**: File paper documents at the Clerk’s Office, Suite 106, 1 Hamilton County Square, Noblesville. Hours are typically Monday–Friday, roughly 8:00 a.m.–4:00/4:30 p.m. (confirm current hours). Phone: 317-776-9629. ### After Filing - **Serve your spouse**: Options include certified mail, sheriff, private process server, or a Waiver of Service if they cooperate. Proof of service must be filed with the court. - Track your case free on **MyCase**: **https://mycase.in.gov** - Complete any required parenting classes if minor children are involved. - After the 60-day wait, you can seek a final hearing or (in fully agreed cases) a summary decree without a hearing if the paperwork is in order. ### Important Notes and Caveats - **Self-representation risks**: Divorce involves property division (Indiana is equitable distribution / “one-pot”), debts, support, custody, and long-term consequences. The Self-Help Center and court staff **cannot** give legal advice. Consider at least a consultation with a local family law attorney, especially if children, significant assets, retirement accounts, or disagreement exist. - Local rules apply in Hamilton County (financial declarations, parenting education, etc.). The Self-Help Center or clerk can point you to them. - Online document-preparation services exist (they generate forms for a fee), but you still handle actual filing and service. Official free forms from indianalegalhelp.org are the safest starting point. - Fees, available case types for e-filing, and local procedures can change—always verify directly with the Hamilton County Clerk or Self-Help Center. **Primary contacts & links**: - Hamilton County Clerk: 1 Hamilton County Square, Suite 106, Noblesville, IN 46060 | 317-776-9629 - Legal Self-Help Center: hamiltoncounty.in.gov/1133/Legal-Self-Help-Center - Free forms: indianalegalhelp.org - E-filing: in.gov/courts/efile - Case search: mycase.in.gov Start with the residency check and the correct form packet on indianalegalhelp.org, then contact the Self-Help Center for e-filing help. That is the most practical path for filing online (or mostly online) in Noblesville.

8/31/26 3:50pm L: Several things can make someone a difficult spouse without making them an unfit parent. For example: She cheated on her husband. She has a new boyfriend. She has little or no income. She is unemployed. She receives public assistance. She wants to move to another state. She has ADHD. She takes legitimately prescribed medication. She has debt. She doesn't get along with the father. She wants a divorce. She makes parenting decisions the father disagrees with. She has a different parenting philosophy. Those facts can become relevant if they produce an actual risk to the children, but the fact itself does not automatically establish parental unfitness. Indiana's statutory framework focuses on the children's best interests and requires consideration of all relevant circumstances rather than applying an automatic presumption against one parent.
8/31/26 3:52pm L: How visitation could work with Indiana/California distance Indiana's Parenting Time Guidelines specifically address situations where distance is a major factor. For children age 5 or older attending a traditional school calendar, the guideline model contemplates approximately: 7 weeks of summer vacation with the noncustodial parent. 7 days during winter vacation. The entire spring break. Additional parenting time when the father is visiting the children's area or the children are visiting his area. That is a guideline, not an automatic California schedule. The actual order can be customized. For example, a practical long-distance arrangement could look something like: Mother: California primary residence Normal school year Father: Connecticut Summer: Approximately 6–8 weeks with father Winter: Approximately 1 week Spring: Entire school spring break Holidays: Alternating major holidays where practical Communication: Regular scheduled video/telephone contact Transportation: Specific provisions identifying who purchases flights, who accompanies younger children, and where exchanges occur The court can allocate transportation expenses differently depending on the circumstances. Indiana's guidelines specifically recognize travel costs, employment schedules, financial circumstances, and frequency of parenting time as relevant considerations when distance is substantial.
